IV. Alternatives to the Proposed Action
A) No Action:
Selection of this alternative would amount to maintaining the status quo position on Interior lands, which is one rife with problems. Actually, the status quo is not static; it is a dynamic condition which can be characterized by the increasing popularity of ORV and increasing use of such vehicles on the public lands. Use of these vehicles has reached such proportions that some land managers charged with stewardship of the public resources are finding themselves in untenable positions as regards their primary responsibilities.
Taking the "no action" course would result in the following impacts:
There would be a continuation of the degradation of the surficial resources of the public lands.
There would be more and more widespread instances of ORV disruption of ecological communities on the public lands.
"No action" would allow the continuance on public lands of situations which subject the ORV rider to hazards stemming from unsafe operation and/or unsafe vehicle condition. Accidents involving use of ORV are on the increase. A complicating aspect of arresting this problem, on the public lands, is the fact that many visitors are urban dwellers unfamiliar with the hazards of the open country. Another is the large number of public land hazards remaining from the days when these lands were quite remote and inaccessible; abandoned mining shafts and open pits are examples of such remaining hazards.
Failure to act would permit the many and varied present problems of littering, interference with livestock operations and vandalism and other crimes to continue on extensive areas of the public lands. Under present Departmental manpower limitations, these problems pose unmanageable situations which could be ameliorated in some instances by making known to the public what specific areas have been designated as open — and appropriate for ORV use.
